title: GCD of the First Odds and Evens
statement:
You get a positive integer n. Let A be the sum of the first n odd positive integers (1, 3, 5, …) and B the sum of the first n even positive integers (2, 4, 6, …).

Return the greatest common divisor of A and B.
hints: Write out the two sums for small n. Do you recognise them?
The first n odd numbers add up to n², and the first n even numbers add up to n(n + 1).
gcd(n·n, n·(n + 1)) = n · gcd(n, n + 1). What is the gcd of two consecutive integers?

explain.intuition:
Both sums have closed forms. Odd numbers stack into squares: 1, 1+3 = 4, 1+3+5 = 9, so A = n². Each even number is twice a counting number, so B = 2 · n(n + 1)/2 = n(n + 1).

Now pull out the common factor: gcd(n · n, n · (n + 1)) = n · gcd(n, n + 1). Consecutive integers share no factor (any common divisor would also divide their difference, 1), so the inner gcd is 1. The answer is just n. Computing the sums directly also works for small inputs but the products reach 1018, beyond exact double precision in JavaScript.
steps: Sum of the first n odd numbers: n².
Sum of the first n even numbers: n(n + 1).
Factor out n: the gcd is n · gcd(n, n + 1).
Consecutive integers are coprime, so return n.
pitfalls: Looping up to n to add the numbers. At n = 10⁹ that is far too slow.
Computing n² and n(n + 1) in JavaScript numbers for large n. Above about 9·10<sup>15</sup> the values are no longer exact, so the gcd can come out wrong.
Assuming the answer must be small because gcds of unrelated numbers usually are. Here the two sums share the factor n by construction.

solutions.title: Add the numbers, then Euclid
solutions.idea: Build both sums with a loop and run the Euclidean algorithm on them.

solutions.title: Closed forms factor to n
solutions.idea: A = n² and B = n(n + 1). Their gcd is n times gcd(n, n + 1), and consecutive integers are coprime.

followups: Return the gcd of the sum of the first n odd numbers and the sum of the first m even numbers, with n ≠ m.
Prove gcd(a·c, b·c) = c·gcd(a, b) using the Euclidean algorithm.
